claims.text: Aluminum enrichment can be introduced into the near-surface region of a refractory high-entropy alloy by surface pre-alloying or infusion.
Surface aluminum enrichment will promote formation of an Al2O3 scale during high-temperature oxygen exposure.
The resulting Al2O3 scale will be continuous, adherent, and slow-growing.
Added surface aluminum preferentially oxidizes at high temperature to form Al2O3.
The Al2O3 layer acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Slower oxygen ingress reduces subsequent oxidation of the underlying alloy.
Aluminum enrichment will improve the alloy's overall high-temperature oxygen resistance.
Under exposure at approximately 1200°C in air at about 0.21 atm oxygen partial pressure for 100 hours, the treated alloy will have lower oxidation-induced weight gain than the untreated alloy.
Under the specified exposure, the treated alloy will retain better structural integrity than the untreated alloy.
Under the specified exposure, the treated alloy will exhibit a more protective oxide layer than the untreated alloy.
Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys typically form less-protective or non-continuous oxide scales.
The oxide scales formed by the untreated alloy permit more rapid oxidation and degradation under extreme-temperature exposure.
The benefit requires an aluminum concentration sufficient to form a stable Al2O3 layer.
The intervention should not adversely affect the core mechanical properties of the alloy.
Insufficient aluminum enrichment may prevent the expected oxidation-resistance benefit.
Temperatures outside the stated stability range of Al2O3 may prevent the expected benefit.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant oxidation reduction, formation of a non-continuous or non-adherent Al2O3 scale, or degradation of mechanical properties relative to the untreated control would falsify the hypothesis.
